name: cycle

capacity.note: under three there is no loop to read; past six the ring crowds

density.note: a stage is a name plus one clause, not a paragraph

description: A closed loop of 3-6 stages that returns to its start — for a process with no beginning or end, where the last stage feeds the first.
purpose: Use when the sequence is CIRCULAR: a natural cycle, a feedback loop, a recurring phase. A linear process with a real start and finish is list-steps; a cycle's whole point is the return.

stages.description: Each list item is one stage in the loop. Top bullet = stage name (auto-bold); one nested bullet = a single clause of body. Read clockwise; the last stage returns to the first.

sample:
<!-- _class: cycle -->

`The water cycle`

## Nothing is spent — only moved.

- Evaporation
  - The sun lifts water from ocean and leaf into vapor.
- Condensation
  - Vapor cools into cloud, a reservoir held aloft.
- Precipitation
  - Rain and snow return the water to the ground.
- Collection
  - Rivers gather it back to the sea, and it begins again.

stressDoc.summary: Six stages — the last legible ring.
stressDoc.sample:
<!-- _class: cycle -->

`The carbon cycle`

## Six stages is the crowded ceiling.

- Photosynthesis
  - Plants pull carbon from the air into sugar.
- Respiration
  - Living things burn sugar and breathe carbon back.
- Decomposition
  - Decay returns carbon from the dead to the soil.
- Combustion
  - Fire and fuel release stored carbon at once.
- Ocean uptake
  - Seawater absorbs a share of the airborne carbon.
- Sedimentation
  - The slow route locks carbon into stone, and the wheel turns.

whenToUse.title: The sequence is circular
whenToUse.body: When the last stage feeds the first and there is no true beginning — a natural cycle, a feedback loop, a recurring season. The return is the point; a layout with a start and end would misrepresent it.

whenToUse.title: Three to six stages
whenToUse.body: Under three there is no loop to trace; past six the ring crowds and the return arc loses force. Merge adjacent stages or move to list-steps.

whenToUse.title: Each stage is a name plus a clause
whenToUse.body: A stage carries a short name (auto-bold) and one clause of body. Richer per-stage descriptions belong in list-steps; a bare list of names belongs in list.

antiPatterns.title: A linear process
antiPatterns.body: If the sequence has a real start and a real end, use list-steps — the numbered spine promises exactly that order. The cycle's closed loop mis-cues a one-way process as recurring.

antiPatterns.title: More than six stages
antiPatterns.body: Past six the ring crowds and the descriptions shrink below legibility. Keep the six load-bearing stages here and push the detail to list-steps or a second slide.

antiPatterns.title: Parallel options
antiPatterns.body: If the items are alternatives the audience weighs rather than stages that flow into each other, use cards-grid or verdict-grid. The arrows here read as causation, not choice.

related.name: list-steps
related.when: the process is linear — a real start and finish, not a loop

related.name: timeline-list
related.when: events fixed to dates rather than a repeating cycle

related.name: diagram
related.when: the loop has branches or feedback into non-adjacent stages

commonMistakes.mistake: Authoring stages as a numbered list (`1.`) instead of a bullet list (`-`).
commonMistakes.fix: The stage-node styling and connector chevrons are scoped to `ul > li` (`section.cycle > .cell-stage > ul`) — an `ol` doesn't match the selector, so stages render as a plain, unstyled numbered list with no ring, no chevrons, no return arc.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming the eyebrow follows the after-heading pattern used by `title`/`closing`.
commonMistakes.fix: cycle has no eyebrow-specific CSS — it inherits the shared before-heading rule (base.modifiers.css): the inline-code eyebrow paragraph must sit directly BEFORE the `## heading`, not after it, or the masthead lift re-seats it as the italic, secondary-color subtitle instead of the intended mono kicker.
